hints.junior: A scroll handler runs on every scroll event, which can fire far more often than the screen can repaint. That mismatch is what makes scrolling feel sticky.
hints.mid: Scroll events can fire 100+ times a second on a fast trackpad or fling gesture — way past the ~60 times a second the browser can actually paint.
hints.staff: requestAnimationFrame throttling ties your handler to the paint cycle itself, not a guessed millisecond constant, so it adapts to whatever refresh rate the display actually supports.

hints.junior: Watch the event counter in 'broken' mode climb fast during a scroll. In 'fixed' mode, the actual work only runs once per frame no matter how many raw events fired.
hints.mid: The raw scroll-event count is identical in both modes — only how often the handler does real work differs.
hints.staff: Both modes log the raw event count and the actual-work count separately, so the coalescing ratio is directly visible, not just claimed.

hints.junior: Set a flag when a scroll happens, then check it once per animation frame — that turns any number of scroll events into at most one real update.
hints.mid: The tick-flag plus rAF pattern is the standard way to throttle high-frequency DOM events to the paint cycle without a fixed-timing debounce/throttle utility.
hints.staff: Unlike a millisecond-based throttle, rAF-based coalescing self-adjusts to the display refresh rate — 60Hz, 120Hz, whatever the device actually paints at.

hints.junior: Add { passive: true } to scroll listeners that never call preventDefault — it lets the browser start scrolling immediately instead of waiting on your handler.
hints.mid: Cancel any pending requestAnimationFrame handle on cleanup with cancelAnimationFrame, so a queued frame never runs against DOM nodes that are already gone.
hints.staff: Read layout-dependent values like scrollY inside the rAF callback, not the raw scroll handler, to avoid racing the browser’s own scroll-position bookkeeping.

sections.junior: Hey! Today we're fixing a scroll handler that runs way more often than it needs to, making the page feel sticky while you scroll.
sections.mid: This case covers throttling scroll handlers to the animation frame cycle instead of running on every raw scroll event.
sections.staff: We're covering the tick-flag rAF pattern, passive listeners, and reading layout values safely inside a throttled scroll handler.

sections.junior: Set a flag on scroll, then do the real work once per animation frame. Any number of scroll events between frames collapses into one update.
sections.mid: The rAF-based pattern ties your throttle to the actual paint cycle, not a guessed timing constant, so it adapts to the display’s real refresh rate.
sections.staff: This differs from a fixed-millisecond debounce or throttle utility precisely because it’s tied to paint timing, not a constant.

sections.junior: Watch the counters: raw scroll events climb fast, but the actual work counter barely moves in fixed mode. That's the coalescing in action.
sections.mid: Both modes log the raw event count separately from the actual-work count, so you can see the coalescing ratio directly.
sections.staff: Open DevTools Performance while scrolling in each mode to compare the number of script-execution blocks tied to the handler.

sections.junior: Don't do real work inside a raw scroll handler. Set a flag, and do the work once per animation frame instead.
sections.mid: The tick-flag plus requestAnimationFrame pattern coalesces any number of scroll events between frames into a single update.
sections.staff: Always add passive true to scroll listeners that never call preventDefault, and cancel any pending animation frame on cleanup.
